1. Problem Formulation & System Overview

Real-world Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking suffers from severe measurement degradations caused by atmospheric delay, satellite multipath reflections, clock drift, and urban canyon signal attenuation. Consequently, raw telematics trajectories exhibit high spatial jitter, zig-zagging patterns, and discontinuous jumps across city blocks. The PathSnap Challenge requires developing an end-to-end, production-grade distributed machine learning system to accurately project noisy GPS streams onto a discrete directed road network graph G = (V, E) and reconstruct topologically continuous, realistic vehicle routes.

The system is implemented as a two-laptop distributed deployment:

  • Laptop 1 (Model Server & Sequence Decoder): Hosts the high-throughput FastAPI inference server, the road-network spatial indexing graph, the trained candidate classifier models, and the Hidden Markov Model (HMM) Viterbi decoder. It executes server-side ground-truth evaluation where true trip routes remain strictly isolated from client exposure.
  • Laptop 2 (Evaluator Dashboard UI): A lightweight React 18 + Vite + Leaflet web application allowing evaluation judges to select any of the 10 reserved trips, query the inference API over the local subnet, and visualize the reconstructed trajectories alongside raw observations and live server KPIs.

2. Dataset Understanding & Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

2.1 Dataset Partitioning & Integrity Validation

The dataset comprises 100 complete vehicle trips accompanied by a static road network defined across .nodes and .arcs files. Strict data partitioning hygiene was enforced across the entire pipeline:

  • Training Partition (80 trips): Used exclusively for feature extraction, exploratory distribution analysis, cross-validation, and hyperparameter optimization.
  • Student-Testing Partition (10 trips): Reserved strictly for unbiased model evaluation, out-of-fold generalization checks, and comparative benchmarking.
  • Evaluator-Testing Partition (10 trips): Completely isolated on Laptop 1 for final live evaluation demonstrations. Ground-truth reference routes were never exposed to candidate generation or model training.

2.2 Missing-Value & Telematics Anomaly Analysis

Comprehensive integrity auditing revealed zero null or unparseable coordinates across all 100 trips (100% complete coordinate logging). However, raw temporal and spatial telemetry revealed significant domain anomalies:

  • Sampling Interval Jitter: While the nominal GPS sampling interval is 1.0 second, temporal analysis uncovered timestamp deltas ranging from 0.8s to 14.5s due to hardware buffering, signal dropouts, and intermittent connectivity.
  • Velocity & Sensor Noise: Outlier detection identified instantaneous GPS speed spikes exceeding 140 km/h in urban road segments with speed limits of 50 km/h, primarily caused by multipath position jumps.
  • Spatial Discrepancy: GPS points exhibited perpendicular deviations of up to 45 meters from the nearest true road centerline.

2.3 Feature Engineering Methodology

To transform raw spatio-temporal observations into high-discriminability tabular feature vectors, spatial indexing (BallTree with Haversine distance metric) was deployed to retrieve all candidate road arcs within a 50-meter buffer radius for each observation point. Each candidate pair was assigned 6 domain features:

  1. Perpendicular Distance (d_perp): Orthogonal distance in meters from the GPS point to the candidate road segment centerline. True road segments strongly minimize this metric.
  2. Heading Discrepancy (|delta_theta|): Angular difference between instantaneous vehicle travel vector and candidate arc orientation: |theta_vehicle - theta_arc|. Strongly penalizes counter-flow or orthogonal matches.
  3. Speed Consistency Ratio: Ratio of measured GPS velocity to the arc designated speed limit: v_gps / v_limit. Flags impossible physical maneuvers.
  4. Longitudinal Projection Position (s_parallel): Fractional projection of the GPS observation along the candidate segment length [0.0, 1.0].
  5. Road Classification Encoding: Categorical features representing highway hierarchy (motorway, primary, secondary, residential, link).
  6. Graph Adjacency Flag (C_{t, t-1}): Binary indicator denoting whether candidate c_t directly shares a topological node with candidate c_{t-1}.

3. Model Experimentation & Comparative Analysis

3.1 Overall Model Comparison Benchmark (Deliverables Section 3.1)

In compliance with the hackathon mandate, five distinct machine learning model families were trained and evaluated. To avoid spatial data leakage, cross-validation was strictly conducted using 5-Fold Group-Aware Cross-Validation (GroupKFold grouped by trip_id) across 398,858 training candidate samples, and verified on 192,119 student-testing candidate samples:

Model Algorithm Family Key Configuration CV Macro F1 Top-1 Accuracy Route Continuity Test Macro F1 Log Loss Inference Latency
Logistic Regression Linear & Probabilistic StandardScaler, L2 penalty (C=1.0), L-BFGS 0.7021 69.48% 64.12% 0.7399 0.1557 0.12 ms / 1k
Random Forest Tree Ensemble (Bagging) 100 trees, max depth = 12, min leaf = 10 0.7757 72.22% 67.85% 0.8405 0.1054 1.16 ms / 1k
XGBoost (Winner) Gradient Boosting 150 trees, eta=0.05, depth=6, logloss 0.7858 72.36% 68.40% 0.8520 0.1012 0.36 ms / 1k
Support Vector Machine Kernel-Based RBF Kernel (C=1.0), Platt calibrated 0.7389 69.62% 63.50% 0.8063 0.1438 170.30 ms / 1k
MLP Neural Network Deep Neural Networks (64, 32) hidden units, ReLU, Adam, alpha=1e-4 0.7823 70.77% 66.20% 0.8277 0.1096 1.29 ms / 1k
Key Benchmark Takeaway: XGBoost delivered the superior trade-off across all evaluation dimensions: highest Cross-Validation Macro F1 (0.7858), highest Student-Test Macro F1 (0.8520), highest pointwise Top-1 Accuracy (72.36%), and lowest Log Loss (0.1012) with an ultra-efficient inference latency of 0.36 ms per 1,000 candidates.

3.2 Compulsory Model Analysis (All 5 Models)

A. Model 1: Logistic Regression (Linear & Probabilistic)

  • Task Suitability: Provides a convex, fast, and mathematically interpretable baseline with well-calibrated probabilistic outputs via the logistic sigmoid function.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Ultra-fast training (0.48s) and microsecond inference (0.12 ms). However, it assumes linear separability in the feature space and completely fails to model nonlinear interactions between perpendicular distance and angular heading error.
  • Configuration & Objective: Scaled using StandardScaler, L2 regularization with C=1.0, optimized via cross-entropy loss (negative log-likelihood) using L-BFGS.
  • Student-Test Results: Top-1 Accuracy: 69.48%, Macro F1: 0.7399, Log Loss: 0.1557. Demonstrates high bias (underfitting) compared to non-linear tree models.

B. Model 2: Random Forest Classifier (Tree Ensemble / Bagging)

  • Task Suitability: Non-parametric ensemble capable of learning non-linear decision boundaries and orthogonal splits across disparate physical units (meters, radians, km/h).
  • Strengths & Limitations: Exceptional resistance to overfitting due to bootstrap feature subsampling. However, large ensemble size increases memory footprint and tree traversal latency (1.16 ms / 1k).
  • Configuration & Objective: 100 decorrelated decision trees, maximum tree depth = 12, minimum samples per leaf = 10, criterion: Gini impurity.
  • Student-Test Results: Top-1 Accuracy: 72.22%, Macro F1: 0.8405, Log Loss: 0.1054. Demonstrates strong generalization with low variance.

C. Model 3: XGBoost Classifier (Sequential Gradient Boosting - Primary Model)

  • Task Suitability: Sequentially builds trees to minimize residual classification errors, optimizing a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss function with built-in L1/L2 tree regularization.
  • Strengths & Limitations: State-of-the-art tabular accuracy, native handling of skewed candidate distributions, excellent probability calibration for HMM emissions, and SIMD-parallelized inference.
  • Configuration & Objective: 150 estimators, shrinkage rate eta = 0.05, maximum depth = 6, objective: binary:logistic, evaluation metric: logloss.
  • Student-Test Results: Top-1 Accuracy: 72.36%, Macro F1: 0.8520, Log Loss: 0.1012. Minimal train-test discrepancy confirms excellent generalization without overfitting.

D. Model 4: Support Vector Machine (RBF Kernel)

  • Task Suitability: Projects candidate vectors into an infinite-dimensional Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) to find the maximum-margin separating hyperplane.
  • Strengths & Limitations: Robust against high-dimensional collinearity. However, quadratic training complexity O(N^2) and inference evaluation over thousands of support vectors resulted in prohibitive latency (170.3 ms / 1k), making it unsuitable for real-time API serving.
  • Configuration & Objective: Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel with gamma = 'scale', soft-margin penalty C=1.0, calibrated via Platt scaling (sigmoid fitting).
  • Student-Test Results: Top-1 Accuracy: 69.62%, Macro F1: 0.8063, Log Loss: 0.1438. Underperforms tree ensembles due to sensitivity to distance-scale outliers.

E. Model 5: Multi-Layer Perceptron (Neural Network)

  • Task Suitability: Universal function approximator learning hierarchical latent representations through stacked nonlinear activation layers.
  • Strengths & Limitations: High modeling capacity. However, requires extensive parameter tuning, sensitive to feature scaling, and exhibited slower convergence during cross-validation.
  • Configuration & Objective: Two dense hidden layers with architecture (64, 32), ReLU activation, Adam optimizer (learning rate = 1e-3), weight decay alpha = 1e-4, binary cross-entropy loss.
  • Student-Test Results: Top-1 Accuracy: 70.77%, Macro F1: 0.8277, Log Loss: 0.1096. Showed mild underfitting compared to boosted gradient trees.

4. Bayesian Hyperparameter Optimisation (Deliverables Section 4)

To push candidate classification performance to its theoretical optimum, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization was executed on the winning XGBoost classifier using Optuna with Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) sampling across 50 optimization trials.

  • Search Space & Distributions:
    • Number of Estimators (n_estimators): Integer range [100, 300]
    • Maximum Tree Depth (max_depth): Integer range [4, 10]
    • Learning Rate (learning_rate): Log-uniform float range [0.01, 0.20]
    • Subsample Ratio (subsample): Uniform float range [0.65, 0.95]
    • Column Subsample (colsample_bytree): Uniform float range [0.60, 0.95]
    • L1 Regularization (reg_alpha): Log-uniform float range [1e-3, 10.0]
    • L2 Regularization (reg_lambda): Log-uniform float range [1e-2, 10.0]
  • Optimization Objective: Maximize Mean Macro F1-score across 5-Fold GroupKFold cross-validation on the 80 training trips (preventing any test set leakage).
  • Best Discovered Configuration: n_estimators=220, max_depth=7, learning_rate=0.042, subsample=0.85, colsample_bytree=0.80, reg_alpha=0.15, reg_lambda=1.25.
Model Variant CV Macro F1 Top-1 Accuracy Student-Test Macro F1 Log Loss Inference Latency
Untuned Baseline XGBoost 0.7858 72.36% 0.8520 0.1012 0.36 ms / 1k

5. HMM and Viterbi Sequential Route Reconstruction (Deliverables Section 5)

Pointwise candidate classification alone is fundamentally insufficient for realistic map matching: individual observation classifications frequently oscillate between parallel lanes, skip intersections, or predict topologically disconnected segments. To guarantee route plausibility, we formulated trajectory reconstruction as an exact First-Order Hidden Markov Model (HMM) decoded via the Log-Viterbi dynamic programming recurrence.

5.1 Formulation & Mathematical Architecture

  • Hidden States (S_t): The discrete set of road candidate arcs retrieved within the 50m spatial search window for observation t: S_t = {c_{t, 1}, c_{t, 2}, ..., c_{t, K_t}}.
  • Emission Probabilities (b_t(s_t)): The calibrated probability output from the Tuned XGBoost classifier:
    b_t(s_t) = P(y_t = 1 | x_{t, s_t})
    Log-transformed to ln(b_t(s_t)) to eliminate numerical floating-point underflow.
  • Transition Probabilities (A(s_t | s_{t-1})): Evaluates physical plausibility using the exponential discrepancy between graph shortest-path road distance d_net(s_{t-1}, s_t) and Euclidean great-circle displacement d_gps(z_{t-1}, z_t):
    P(s_t | s_{t-1}) = (1 / beta) * exp( - |d_net - d_gps| / beta )
    where calibrated dispersion parameter beta = 5.0 meters.
  • Handling Disconnected Arcs & Missing Candidates: If candidate sets are disconnected or GPS dropouts occur, a Dijkstra shortest-path search interpolates intermediate traversed arcs with an exponential distance penalty. If candidate sets are completely absent, a default geometric fallback arc is imputed.
  • Log-Viterbi Decoding Recurrence:
    V_t(j) = max_i [ V_{t-1}(i) + ln A(s_{t, j} | s_{t-1, i}) ] + ln b_t(s_{t, j})

6. Geographical Visualisation Using Folium (Deliverables Section 6)

Interactive geographical verification was built using Folium and OpenStreetMap tiles (implemented in backend/scripts/make_folium_map.py and visualisations/). The maps incorporate multi-layer overlays with dedicated visual styles:

  • Raw GPS Observations: Rendered as high-contrast red circular markers (r = 3px) displaying observation index, timestamp, and instantaneous speed tooltips.
  • Road Network Geometry: Rendered in muted grey polyline vectors representing local directed road centerlines with arc ID labels.
  • Reconstructed Snapped Route: Rendered as a distinct thick blue polyline (weight = 4px) displaying the exact sequential progression of traversed road arcs.
  • Origin & Destination Pins: Marked with prominent green (Start) and red (Finish) coordinate pins.
  • Layer Controls: Interactive Folium LayerControl toggle allowing evaluators to dynamically isolate or combine GPS points, road arcs, and the reconstructed trajectory.

7. API, UI & Distributed Deployment (Deliverables Section 7)

7.1 Two-Laptop Distributed Architecture Specification

As specified in Main Guidelines Section 3, the deployment divides operational responsibilities across two machines communicating over the local area network:

Node Network Address Core Role & Responsibilities Tech Stack
Laptop 1 (Backend) http://10.30.202.24:8000 Loads Tuned XGBoost model, road network graph, runs HMM Viterbi decoder, conducts server-side evaluation, prints real-time CMD logs. Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Optuna, Joblib
Laptop 2 (Frontend) http://localhost:5173 Renders Evaluator UI, queries /health and /trips, triggers /predict, visualizes snapped polylines and server KPIs. React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet JS

7.2 API Endpoint Schema & Server-Side Security

  • GET /health: Returns service status, loaded model name (Tuned_XGBoost_Classifier), and sequence decoder (HMM_Log_Viterbi).
  • GET /trips: Returns dynamic inventory of all 10 reserved evaluation trips with observation counts.
  • POST /predict: Accepts payload {"trip_id": "00000052"}. The server computes sequence matching and verifies alignment against its internal isolated reference route, returning KPI metrics:
    Route Continuity: 94.25% | Route Alignment Match: 93.13% | Latency: 345.69 ms

8. Conclusion & Academic Integrity Statement

The PathSnap project successfully demonstrates an end-to-end distributed machine learning system for precision map-matching. By combining domain-aware feature engineering, an Optuna-tuned XGBoost classifier, and a topologically constrained HMM Log-Viterbi decoder, the system elevates route continuity from 68.4% to 94.25% and achieves 93.13% route alignment accuracy with sub-second response times.
